melanotan-ii.text: Users inject melanotan II as a sunless tanning shortcut, aiming for darker skin with less sun exposure. It is an unapproved research peptide that also affects libido and appetite. Its tanning effect has been documented in small human studies, while claims of sunburn protection and equivalence with prescription afamelanotide rest largely on anecdote.

afamelanotide.text: Afamelanotide (melanotan I) is a prescription implant approved for a rare light-sensitivity disorder, and tanning communities discuss it as a supposedly gentler relative of melanotan II. The darkening is a side effect of its approved use. Claims about fewer moles or cosmetic use in healthy people are mostly anecdotal.

dihydroxyacetone.text: DHA is the active ingredient in self-tanning lotions, sprays and salon spray tans, used to get a bronzed look without sun exposure. The colour is a temporary surface stain rather than new pigment. Its cosmetic effect is well established; it is not a sunscreen, and application technique is a common forum topic.

chain: Carotenoid deposits in fat under skin
canthaxanthin.text: Canthaxanthin was sold in oral tanning pills to give skin a golden-orange tint, using the same pigment that colours farmed salmon. The colour change is documented, but it is a pigment deposit rather than a true tan, and the pills have drawn regulatory and safety concerns.

beta-carotene.text: Looksmaxxing forums discuss beta-carotene, from food or supplements, as a way to give skin a warmer, golden colour. Studies have measured small skin colour shifts from high carotenoid intake, and some people report an orange cast. Whether the result reads as attractive is a matter of debate among users.

lycopene.text: Lycopene, from cooked tomatoes or supplements, is mentioned in skin and tan communities as a mild internal photoprotectant and a source of a warm, reddish tint. Small trials have looked at UV-induced redness; evidence for visible tanning or lasting appearance changes is limited.

astaxanthin.text: Astaxanthin is taken as a supplement for skin glow, anti-aging and a slightly warmer tone. Some small trials have measured skin moisture, elasticity and UV redness. Its role in estrogen control on TRT is a forum claim that rests on anecdote.

polypodium-leucotomos.text: Users take Polypodium leucotomos extract as an 'internal sunscreen' alongside tanning, or to limit sun-driven dark spots and aging. Small trials have studied reduced sunburn reactions and some pigmentation conditions such as melasma. It is not a replacement for topical sunscreen in the studies.

glutathione.text: Glutathione, oral or injected, is promoted for skin lightening and a brighter complexion, mainly in parts of Asia, and it is also taken as a general antioxidant by lifters. Small trials report modest lightening in some participants, though results are inconsistent and injectable use is largely unregulated.

l-cysteine.text: L-cysteine is discussed as a glutathione precursor that might lighten skin, and also as a building block for hair keratin. It is also used by steroid users for general support. The lightening idea comes from pigment biochemistry and has little direct human evidence for cosmetic use.

tretinoin.text: Tretinoin is the most widely discussed prescription cream in skincare and looksmaxxing circles, used for acne, fine wrinkles, texture and uneven pigment. Its use for acne and photoaging is supported by decades of clinical trials. Early purging and irritation are commonly reported, and users debate how to tolerate them.

chain: Converts to retinoic acid in skin
retinol.text: Retinol is the over-the-counter vitamin A cosmetic, used as a milder alternative to tretinoin for fine lines, texture, acne marks and uneven tone, sometimes around the eyes. Trials support modest anti-aging effects on the face. Under-eye claims about filling dark circles are less studied.

adapalene.text: Adapalene gel is the retinoid sold without a prescription in the US, used for acne on the face, back and shoulders, including testosterone-related breakouts, and for texture. Its acne benefit is established in trials. Use for aging is less studied, and claims that it outperforms tretinoin are not well supported.

tazarotene.text: Tazarotene is a prescription topical retinoid used for acne and photoaging, and forum users describe it as a more intense option than tretinoin. It is studied for acne, psoriasis and fine wrinkles. Reports of heavy peeling and sun sensitivity are common, and claims of a 'feminizing' glow are anecdotal.

isotretinoin.text: Isotretinoin is an oral retinoid prescribed for severe acne and used by people seeking a lasting clear complexion. Its effect on severe acne is well studied. Forum claims include hormonal or mood side effects and combining it with steroids or heavy training, which are discussed largely through anecdote and case reports.

botulinum-toxin-a.text: Botulinum toxin injections are used cosmetically to smooth forehead and eye-area lines and, off-label, to slim the jaw by relaxing the masseter or to reduce clenching. Wrinkle use is approved and well studied. Jaw slimming and facial symmetry uses are less studied, and concerns about a frozen look are commonly discussed.

azelaic-acid.text: Azelaic acid is used in skincare for acne, redness and dark spots, and as a gentler alternative to hydroquinone for melasma. Those skin uses have clinical trial support. Its use as a scalp 'DHT inhibitor' for hair loss, sometimes mixed with minoxidil, is a forum claim with little human evidence.

niacinamide.text: Niacinamide serums and creams are used for oil control, enlarged-looking pores, uneven tone and general skin quality. Trials have studied acne, pigmentation and aging in topical forms. Claims about anxiety, NAD+ energy and TRT symptoms come from oral supplement discussions and are mostly untested for appearance.

vitamin-c-topical.text: Topical vitamin C serums are used to brighten skin, fade dark spots and acne marks, and limit photoaging. Small trials support brightening and some wrinkle improvement. Stability of the formulation, and whether derivatives perform like ascorbic acid, are common forum debates.

tranexamic-acid.text: Tranexamic acid, topical or oral, is used for stubborn melasma and dark marks after acne. It is an approved bleeding drug, so cosmetic use is off-label. Trials in melasma exist, mostly small, and users compare it to hydroquinone, while its use for under-eye darkness is much less studied.

hydroquinone.text: Hydroquinone is a prescription skin lightener used for melasma, sun spots and post-acne marks. Its lightening effect is well documented in clinical studies. Forum discussion centres on safety concerns, regulation in some countries, and reports of long-term high-strength use causing paradoxical darkening.

alpha-arbutin.text: Alpha-arbutin is a cosmetic serum ingredient used to fade dark spots, acne marks and uneven tone, and is marketed as a gentler alternative to hydroquinone. It has some small studies on pigmentation. Evidence for under-eye darkness is thin.

kojic-acid.text: Kojic acid is a fungal-derived ingredient used in brightening creams and soaps for dark spots, acne marks and under-eye darkness. Small studies have looked at melasma. Skin irritation and sensitivity are commonly reported, and evidence for the under-eye use is limited.

cysteamine.text: Cysteamine cream is used as a topical depigmenting agent for melasma and dark spots, sometimes discussed as an alternative to hydroquinone. Its main medical use is a rare metabolic disease. Several small to moderate trials in melasma exist, while use in healthy skin is less studied.

chain: Dissolves oil and dead skin in pores
salicylic-acid.text: Salicylic acid washes and leave-ons are used for blackheads, body acne, steroid-related breakouts, and preventing ingrown hairs after shaving. Its use for acne is established in clinical practice. Scalp and hair-quality uses are for dandruff. Users also report dryness and burning with strong products.

glycolic-acid.text: Glycolic acid is used as an exfoliant for dullness, texture, dark spots, acne marks and fine lines, in home products and professional peels. Trials support modest texture and photoaging improvements. Users often debate strength and frequency, and stronger products are commonly reported to irritate.

lactic-acid.text: Lactic acid is used as a milder exfoliating acid for texture, dullness, uneven tone and dry body skin, in serums and peels. It is a common ingredient in moisturizers for rough skin. Controlled evidence for its appearance effects is more limited than for glycolic acid.

ceramides.text: Ceramide moisturizers are used to repair a damaged skin barrier, especially alongside retinoids and exfoliating acids, giving less dryness and flaking. Their moisturizing role is supported in dermatology studies of dry and eczema-prone skin. Anti-aging claims are mostly indirect.

urea.text: Urea creams are used for rough, dry or bumpy skin on the body and feet, and sometimes for keratosis pilaris texture. Its moisturizing and mild keratolytic role is established in dermatology. Facial anti-aging use is less common and little studied.

chain: Smoother-looking skin and fewer fine lines
hyaluronic-acid.text: Hyaluronic acid serums are used for temporary hydration and plumping, while injectable fillers are used to reshape lips, cheeks and the under-eye area. Topical use gives short-lived surface hydration in studies, and fillers have extensive clinical use for volume. Users often pair it with other actives.
